ra: Ephrem is the paradigmatic Syriac Father, the central figure of Brock's study of the tradition.
Aphrahat, the Persian Sage, is the earliest of the Syriac Fathers grouped in the collective.
Isaac of Nineveh is a principal East Syriac monastic Father.
Jacob of Serugh is a leading West Syriac poet-Father.
Narsai is the chief poet-theologian of the East Syriac Fathers.
Babai the Great is a foundational East Syriac systematic theologian.
Bar Hebraeus is the last great classical Syriac Father and polymath.
John of Ephesus, West Syriac historian-bishop, belongs to the Syriac Fathers.
Philoxenus of Mabbug is a major Miaphysite Syriac Father.
Bardaisan is an early Edessene Syriac thinker counted among the tradition's foundational (if later contested) figures.
Addai is the traditional apostolic founder placed at the head of the Syriac line.
Babai the Great's dyophysite theology continues the Antiochene-Nisibene school transmitted through Narsai's School of Nisibis (Baum-Winkler).
Ephrem's Prose Refutations and hymns explicitly polemicize against Mani and the Manichaeans (Brock).
Ephrem composed hymns against the teaching of Bardaisan and his son Harmonius (Brock).
The Syriac Fathers articulate Christian theology and devotion centered on Jesus Christ, preserved in his own Aramaic tongue.
Isaac of Nineveh's ascetical mysticism stands in the desert-monastic tradition typified by Anthony the Great.
Later tradition links Ephrem with Basil the Great (a legendary meeting); both received as ecumenical doctors.
